def: The principle of Replacement, Reduction and Refinement in animal experimentation: replacing animals with other methods whenever possible, using the smallest number of animals, and reducing as far as possible the pain and stress of those used.
com: It was proposed by the British scientists William Russell and Rex Burch in the book *The Principles of Humane Experimental Technique* (1959). Today it is written into laws such as the 2010 European directive, which states full replacement of animals as its ultimate goal, and Brazil's Arouca Law. Critics say that, in practice, refinement and reduction get more attention than replacement. See Replacement methods, Arouca Law and Animal model.

def: The killing of animals, carried out for consumption and also in other contexts, such as culling herds or for sanitary or population control.
com: The term is also used, euphemistically, for the killing of people in wars and massacres, as if it were justifiable. In every case, the central focus of the debates is the suffering and the harm of death.

def: A method of slaughter that seeks to minimize the animal's suffering, usually by prior stunning; the term is contested by abolitionists, who regard it as an oxymoron.
com: In practice, stunning fails in a share of animals, the speed of slaughter lines makes it hard to correct these failures, and several countries allow exemptions for religious slaughter without stunning. The term also diverts attention from the central fact: the animal is killed without need, almost always very young. See Stunning of animals, Oxymoron and Humane washing.

def: The killing of an animal before it reaches maturity or full productive age, common in some production chains (e.g. male calves in the dairy industry).
com: The name suggests there is a normal age of slaughter, but in livestock farming almost all animals are already killed very young compared with how long they could live: broiler chickens at about six weeks, pigs at five to six months and dairy cows at four to five years, in a species that can live 15 to 20 years. The cases called premature are those in which the animal never even acquires commercial value, such as male calves of dairy breeds, killed at days or weeks of age, and male chicks of laying strains, killed on their first day. See Veal, Dairy industry and Hatchery.

def: A movement to abolish an institution considered unjust; in the historical sense, the movement to end the enslavement of people, above all Black people, in the 18th and 19th centuries; in animal ethics, the current that advocates ending the use of animals as property, rather than reforms that merely regulate that use.
com: The original meaning is the fight against slavery. In Britain, campaigners such as Olaudah Equiano, who had been enslaved, and William Wilberforce helped end the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in most of the empire in 1833; in the United States, Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman were among its best-known figures, and slavery was abolished in 1865. In Brazil, the movement included Luiz Gama, who had been enslaved and, as a lawyer, helped free hundreds of people, and led to the Golden Law of 1888, which made Brazil the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery. Many abolitionists, especially Black abolitionists, also fought racism, which is why abolitionism is seen as part of the history of anti-racist struggle; but not all of them did, and the end of slavery came without reparation or integration, which helps explain inequalities that persist. Today the word also names prison abolitionism, which advocates replacing prisons with other responses. In animal ethics, the term was adopted deliberately, especially by the legal scholar Gary Francione from the 1990s, to argue for ending the property status of animals and to criticize welfarism. This analogy with human slavery is controversial, and using it calls for respect for the word's origin. See Abolitionist veganism, Animal slavery, Welfarism and Reformism.

def: Any deliberate conduct of a moral agent, evaluated ethically by its consequences, intentions or conformity to rules.
com: Under the equal consideration of interests, actions that cause avoidable suffering to sentient beings are subject to the same moral scrutiny applied to actions that affect humans.

def: Direct intervention against animal exploitation, sometimes outside the law (e.g. rescues, sabotage).
com: The best-known example is the Animal Liberation Front (ALF), which emerged in the United Kingdom in 1976, claims rescues and property damage and says it rejects harming any living being. In Brazil, the removal of about 180 beagles from the Instituto Royal in São Roque in 2013 reignited the debate. Governments often treat some of these actions as crime or terrorism, as in the US Animal Enterprise Terrorism Act of 2006, and there is disagreement within the movement about the legitimacy and effectiveness of acting outside the law. See Rescue, Ecoterrorism and Nonviolence.

def: The process of training an animal to perform specific behaviors through conditioning; coercive methods are debated ethically.
com: Methods range from rewards, such as food and play, to punishment, such as leash jerks and shock or prong collars. A study by Ana Catarina Vieira de Castro and colleagues, published in 2020, observed dogs at training schools in Portugal and associated aversive methods with more signs of stress and more pessimistic responses, and several veterinary bodies recommend reward-based training. In circuses, rodeos and other shows, training serves behaviours the animal would not perform on its own, and the criticism goes beyond the method: it questions the use itself. See Animal entertainment and Rodeo.

def: The act of taking on the responsible, permanent care of an animal, usually a rescued or abandoned one, instead of buying it.
com: The slogan "adopt, don't shop" rests on the idea that each purchase encourages commercial breeding, while shelters and rescuers have animals waiting for a home. Adoption solves one animal's situation, but not the cause of abandonment; for that reason it usually comes with neutering and responsible-care campaigns. See Rescue, Animal rescuers (Brazil's "protetores de animais") and Castration.

def: Legal and political work aimed at defending the interests and rights of animals before courts, legislators and public bodies.
com: Part of this advocacy seeks not only to improve conditions of exploitation, but to recognize animals as subjects of rights of their own, and not merely as objects of indirect protection.

def: A strand that centers Black experiences and racial critique within the vegan movement, questioning its predominantly white history.
com: Two works mark this strand: the anthology *Sistah Vegan* (2010), edited by A. Breeze Harper, with writings by Black vegan women, and *Aphro-ism* (2017), by the sisters Aph Ko and Syl Ko. They criticize the idea that veganism is a thing for white and wealthy people and connect the oppression of animals to racism, without treating the two kinds of suffering as equal. See Intersectionality, Intersectional veganism and Animal slavery.

def: A plant-based gelatin extracted from red algae, used as a thickener and a substitute for animal gelatin.
A succulent plant whose nectar is used as a plant-based sweetener alternative to honey.
A being capable of acting morally and of being held responsible for its choices (usually adult humans).
com: Restricting moral agency to humans does not imply that only humans deserve moral consideration: agency and moral patient status are distinct categories. Animals do not need to be agents for their interests to be taken into account.

def: The production of biological tissues (including "meat") from cell culture, without raising and slaughtering animals.
com: Besides cultivated meat, the field includes precision fermentation, in which microorganisms produce proteins identical to animal ones, such as whey or egg-white proteins, without cows or hens. Not every cellular agriculture product does away with animals entirely: cultivated meat still starts from animal cells. See Cultivated meat and Technological veganism.

def: The set of economic activities tied to large-scale agriculture and livestock farming, from production to processing and marketing.
com: It brings together distinct activities: veganism opposes livestock farming and fishing, which are part of agribusiness, but not agriculture, which is also part of it.

def: A tight strap placed around the abdomen of horses or bulls in rodeos to induce bucking, causing discomfort.
com: In Brazil the device is called sedém. Rodeo supporters say it only bothers the animal and does not hurt; critics, such as animal protection organizations, argue that the discomfort is precisely what makes the animal buck, and that the behaviour is not spontaneous. Brazil's Law 10,519/2002 requires cinches and girths to be made of natural wool and bans pointed spurs and electric shocks, but does not ban the flank strap. Pittsburgh, in the United States, banned flank straps at rodeos in 1992, in a city ordinance later overridden by a change in state law. See Rodeo and Vaquejada.

def: A marine plant used in cooking, especially in Asian cuisine, and also a source of iodine and other nutrients.
com: Seaweeds such as nori are sometimes cited as a source of vitamin B12, but many contain forms of the vitamin that the body cannot use, and the content varies greatly between samples. For this reason, nutritionists recommend supplements or fortified foods as a reliable source. Some seaweeds, such as kombu, are also very high in iodine, and excess can be harmful. See Vitamin B12.

def: The distance between people and the real consequences of what they do, produce or consume; in everyday use, also a lack of awareness of what is happening around one.
com: The concept has philosophical roots and gained prominence with Karl Marx, who in the *1844 Manuscripts* described the alienation of workers from the product of their labour. In the consumption of animal products, alienation is made easier by physical and informational distance: animals are kept far away, in closed sheds, death happens out of sight, and meat reaches the shop in pieces that don't look like an animal. The less visible the suffering, the easier it is to keep practices that, seen up close, many people would reject. One caution: calling someone "alienated" tends to sound like an insult and close the conversation; showing what is hidden works better than labelling those who haven't seen it. See Absent referent, Carnism and Cognitive dissonance.

def: A dietary pattern oriented toward promoting physical health, whose content varies with cultural and scientific context; it does not always coincide with ethical vegan choices.
A movement that seeks to maximize the positive impact of actions and resources, including animal welfare as an important cause.
com: Its criteria of scale, neglectedness and tractability tend to favor the animal cause.

def: A view that discusses moral obligations toward the environment, sometimes converging with and sometimes conflicting with animal ethics. Environmentalism can be a moral view or a political movement (see Political environmentalism).
com: It can diverge from a sentientist ethics when it prioritizes the balance of ecosystems or species over the welfare of specific sentient individuals, as in population management policies for wildlife.

def: The removal or prevention of horn growth in cattle, usually by cauterization, in most cases without anesthesia.
com: It is usually done on calves a few weeks old, with a hot iron or caustic paste that burns the horn bud, and studies record signs of pain during and after the procedure. Veterinary bodies, such as the British BVA and BCVA, recommend local anaesthesia and an anti-inflammatory, but surveys of dairy farmers in the United States, Italy and France found that most use no pain relief at all. The reason is management: hornless animals take up less space and injure each other less in crowded groups. Breeding naturally hornless (polled) cattle is pointed to as an alternative. See Dehorning and Anesthesia.

def: An argumentative resource that compares distinct situations because they share relevant characteristics.
com: Comparisons between animal exploitation and human oppressions, such as slavery, are used by antispeciesists to highlight common structures of domination, but they are also criticized for potentially minimizing the specificity and gravity of the historical human suffering involved.

def: A political current that rejects hierarchies and unjustified forms of domination, including the State, and proposes organizing society through voluntary association and self-management.
com: Part of anarchism includes animals: Élisée Reclus defended vegetarianism, and veganarchism, a term coined by Brian A. Dominick (1995), unites veganism and anarchism.

def: A political current that combines the anarchist critique of the State and capitalism with ecological concerns and, at times, animal liberation, rejecting hierarchies between species and forms of domination.
com: By placing speciesism among the forms of domination to be overcome, it comes close to the more radical antispeciesist currents of the animal liberation movement.

def: A medical procedure to suppress the sensation of pain during interventions; its use (or absence) in livestock procedures is a central topic in welfare debates.
com: Several routine procedures in livestock farming are allowed without anaesthesia when performed on very young animals. In the European Union, castration and tail docking of piglets require anaesthesia only after the seventh day of life; in Brazil, the 2020 pig welfare rule of the Ministry of Agriculture requires anaesthesia for tail docking only after the third day and gives farms until 2030 to make it mandatory for all surgical castration. Beak trimming, disbudding and hot-iron branding are also usually done without anaesthesia. Even with local anaesthesia, pain can last for days after the procedure, which is why veterinary bodies also recommend analgesics. See Castration, Tail docking and Beak trimming.

def: A legal and philosophical proposal to recognize certain animals as nonhuman persons, subjects of basic rights, and not mere objects.
com: Restricting this proposal only to species with high cognitive complexity is criticized by sentientists, who argue that the capacity to suffer, not intelligence, should be the relevant criterion for recognizing basic rights.

def: The predominant legal status of animals in most legal systems, which classifies them as movable goods that can be possessed, bought and sold.
com: It is the central target of the abolitionist critique, which argues that, as long as animals are legally property, their fundamental interests can always be legally subordinated to the economic interests of their owners.

def: Species that have adapted to live in urban environments or near humans (rats, pigeons, cockroaches), often treated as pests.
com: Rats, pigeons and cockroaches live near humans because cities offer abundant food, shelter and waste; to a large extent, their presence is a consequence of how humans organize space. For that reason, measures such as waste management and sealing entry points tend to reduce populations more lastingly than killing, which can be followed by recolonization. Living close to humans does not change these animals' capacity to feel. See Pests and Animal population control.

def: A multicellular living being of the kingdom Animalia, capable of movement and, in most cases, possessing a nervous system; a biological term that includes humans, although it is popularly used to refer only to nonhumans.
com: This everyday separation between "humans" and "animals" reinforces, in common language, a moral hierarchy between species that biology itself does not support.

def: An animal that cannot stand up or move because of illness, exhaustion or injury, usually during transport or confinement; a situation associated with serious welfare violations.
com: The industry term is "downer". Because they are hard to move, downed animals may be dragged, pushed or moved with electric shocks to slaughter. In the United States, a 2008 Humane Society video recorded at a California slaughterhouse showed workers using forklifts, water hoses and shocks to force downed cattle to stand, which led to the largest meat recall in the country up to then, about 143 million pounds. In 2009 the US Department of Agriculture banned the slaughter of downed cattle for food, but the rule does not cover pigs and other species. See Live animal transport and Slaughter.

def: An animal kept for emotional and social reasons, with no productive purpose (dogs, cats and other pets).
com: The line between companion and farmed animal is cultural, not biological: dogs are eaten in some countries, guinea pigs are pets in some places and food in others, such as Peru, and pigs can also live as companions. Companion animals receive more affection and legal protection, but they are also bought, sold, bred in large numbers and abandoned. See Pet, Carnism and Selective outrage.

def: An animal raised specifically for slaughter and meat consumption.
com: The expression defines the animal by its function for humans, as if being eaten were one of its traits. Meat strains were selected to grow fast: a broiler chicken reaches slaughter weight in about six weeks, and rapid growth is associated with leg and heart problems. See Farmed animal, Speciesist term and Artificial selection.

def: An animal raised to generate products (meat, milk, eggs, wool) for human consumption or trade.
com: The expression treats the animal's body as a machine that generates products and hides that, in the case of meat, the product is the dead animal itself. It is used in laws and technical standards worldwide, including Brazil, and so appears even in texts on animal welfare. Some people prefer "animal raised for consumption" or "exploited animal", which make clear who benefits. See Meat animal, Speciesist term and Objectification.

def: A species selected and bred over generations under human control, genetically adapted to living with humans or to production (as opposed to a wild animal).
Any animal that is not of the human species, such as mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates.
com: The expression reminds us that human beings are animals too and avoids the opposition "humans and animals", which suggests a greater separation than biology shows and usually comes with the moral exclusion of other animals. It is also written "non-human animal". In everyday writing, "animals" or "other animals" also work, as long as it is clear who is meant. See Animal, Speciesism and Anthropocentrism.

termo: Animalism (in the sense of animal advocacy)
def: A generic term for the set of ideas, movements and practices aimed at defending animals, ranging from welfarism to abolitionism.
com: Because it covers positions as different as welfarism and abolitionism, the term is criticized by stricter antispeciesists for blurring relevant strategic and ethical differences between these currents.

def: Organized opposition to environmental protection policies and movements, often in the name of economic growth, which includes denying or downplaying problems such as climate change.
com: Not every criticism of an environmental measure is antienvironmentalism: someone starting from sentientism, for example, questions measures that harm animals without denying environmental problems.

def: A position and movement that actively opposes speciesism, defending the equal consideration of interests across species.
com: Not every antispeciesist necessarily defends the end of all use of animals, a position more associated with abolitionism; in the strict sense, antispeciesism is the rejection of moral discrimination based on species.

def: The set of positions, discourses, campaigns and measures that oppose veganism, as a philosophy or as a practice.
com: It ranges from jokes and stereotypes to industry campaigns and rules that hinder vegan products, such as the 2017 ruling of the Court of Justice of the European Union that reserved names like "milk" and "cheese" for animal products. The most common anti-vegan arguments are nutritional, cultural and economic. The nutritional ones have lost ground: bodies such as the US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics consider well-planned vegan diets appropriate at all stages of life, though some call for more caution in childhood. See Anti-vegan, Non-vegan and Carnism.

def: The view that places the human being as the center and measure of moral value.
com: It is the worldview that antispeciesism and sentientism most directly contest, because it assigns moral value on the basis of species, and not of the capacity to suffer.

def: The view that only human interests have moral value of their own, and that everything else matters insofar as it serves humans or affects them.
com: It underpins arguments such as "they're just animals." Sentientism rejects it for treating species, and not the capacity to feel, as the criterion.

def: The attribution of human characteristics, emotions or intentions to nonhuman animals; it can be a useful tool of empathy or a source of interpretive error, depending on the scientific context.
com: Categorically rejecting any attribution of mental states to animals, out of fear of anthropomorphism, can fall into the opposite bias: systematically underestimating the mental life of other species.

def: Emotional or motivational indifference in the face of another's suffering.
com: In relation to animals, it tends to work as a psychological mechanism that sustains exploitative practices despite the intellectual recognition that they cause suffering.

def: The keeping of bees to produce honey, wax, propolis and other products, with its own debates about insect sentience and the impact of commercial production.
com: In commercial beekeeping it is common to clip the queen's wings to stop the swarm from leaving, artificially inseminate queens, replace the queen frequently and substitute sugar syrup for the honey removed. Research gathered, for example, in the book *The Mind of a Bee* (2022), by the biologist Lars Chittka, suggests that bees have complex learning and emotion-like states, which makes it plausible that they are sentient, although the question remains open. There are also studies indicating that large numbers of European honeybee hives can compete with native bees for flowers. Most definitions of veganism, such as the Vegan Society's, exclude honey. See Honey, Propolis and Xenospeciesism.

def: The liquid left from cooking chickpeas or other legumes, used as a vegan substitute for egg white because of its foaming properties.
The farming of aquatic animals in captivity, with its own welfare issues that are little regulated.
com: In 2022, according to the FAO, aquaculture overtook capture fisheries for the first time as the main source of aquatic animals, with about 51% of production. A study published in 2023 estimated that about 124 billion farmed fish were killed for food in 2019, not counting shrimp and other crustaceans. Most die by asphyxiation in air or on ice, without stunning, and welfare laws usually protect fish far less than mammals and birds. Farming in dense tanks and net pens also brings disease and parasites and, for carnivorous species such as salmon, the use of wild fish in feed. See Fish farming (pisciculture), Fishing and Industrial fishing.

def: The absence of a consistent rational justification for a distinction or decision.
com: It is identified as the central feature of speciesism: species, taken alone, is not a morally relevant criterion for justifying a difference in treatment.

def: A metal device inserted into the nose of some animals (such as cattle) to make them easier to restrain and lead.
com: The nasal septum is a sensitive area, and the ring works because pulling it causes pain, which makes the animal comply. In bulls it is used to lead large animals; in sows kept outdoors, rings and cuts to the snout are used to stop them from rooting, a natural behaviour of the species. In Brazil, the 2020 pig welfare rule only tolerates snout cutting for this purpose in outdoor sows and with anaesthesia. See Halter, Muzzle and Physical integrity.

def: A structured set of premises that support a conclusion.
com: The strength of an argument about the moral status of animals should be assessed by its logical validity and the evidence that supports it, and not by the familiarity or comfort its conclusion provides.

def: The thesis that only morally relevant characteristics, such as the capacity to suffer, justify a difference in treatment; species, in itself, is not one of those characteristics.
com: It is one of the central arguments used to characterize speciesism as morally unjustified discrimination, analogous to racism and sexism.

def: The thesis that criteria used to exclude animals from moral consideration, such as rationality or language, would also exclude humans with severe cognitive disabilities, revealing an inconsistency in speciesism.
com: Because it exposes this inconsistency, many philosophers consider it one of the hardest challenges to answer for those who defend cognitive criteria as the basis for the moral exclusion of animals.

def: Equipment buckled onto an animal's body for traction, riding or restraint.
A widely cultivated staple cereal, the basis of diets in many cultures and an ingredient in plant-based drinks (rice milk).
The use of art as a tool for activism and awareness-raising.
Organized action in defense of a cause, here the animal cause.
The use of vegan cooking (tastings, food events) as a tool for awareness-raising and conversion to veganism.
A direct, public approach (leafleting, demonstrations, exhibitions).
The use of social media and the internet for mobilization and awareness-raising.
Work through public policy, lobbying and strategic litigation.
The capacity to examine and question one's own beliefs and practices.
com: It is especially relevant for recognizing inconsistencies between declared values, such as rejecting cruelty, and everyday consumption behavior.

def: The right or justification of an agent to react to a threat in order to protect their integrity.
com: Self-defense arguments rarely apply to the routine killing of animals for consumption, since they presuppose a real and proportionate threat, which is absent in most of these practices.

def: The capacity of an agent to govern themselves and make their own decisions.
com: Although often used to deny moral status to animals because of their supposed lack of rational autonomy, this requirement is contested by antispeciesists, who point out that autonomy is not a prerequisite for having interests that deserve consideration: human babies and people with certain severe cognitive disabilities also lack it.

def: The raising of birds (mainly chickens) for meat and egg production.
com: Birds are by far the land animals most killed for food: according to FAO data, more than 70 billion chickens a year, out of a total of more than 80 billion land animals. Broiler chickens are slaughtered at about six weeks; laying hens at around a year and a half, when laying declines; and male chicks of laying strains are killed at hatching. Brazil is one of the largest producers and the largest exporter of chicken meat in the world. See Battery cages, Beak trimming and Hatchery.

def: A cut of cured and smoked pork, traditionally taken from the pig's belly.
Barbed sticks stuck into the bull during a bullfight to provoke and weaken it, causing wounds and intense suffering.
The set of conditions that benefit the collectivity.
com: The systematic exclusion of animals' interests from the definition of what counts as the "common good" is identified by antispeciesists as an arbitrary limitation of this concept to a single species.

def: The state of an animal as regards their health, what they feel and their ability to live according to their nature; also the scientific and ethical field that assesses and seeks to improve that state, especially in animals under human care.
com: The scientist David Fraser described three ways of thinking about welfare: biological functioning (health, growth), affective states (what the animal feels) and natural living (being able to express their behaviors). The three don't always go together: a broiler chicken can grow fast and be in pain. For a sentientist ethics, what the animal feels is central. Animal welfare as a science is not the same as welfarism, the political position that accepts the use of animals as long as they are treated well. See Five Domains, Coping and Welfarism.

def: A position that accepts the use of animals as long as high welfare standards are met, often set against abolitionism in the movement's strategic debate.
com: The best-known criticism comes from the legal scholar Gary Francione, who argued in *Rain Without Thunder* (1996) that welfare reforms make the use of animals more acceptable and prolong it. Supporters of reforms answer that they reduce suffering now, for animals who cannot wait for abolition. Welfarism, as a political position, is not the same as animal welfare, the science that assesses how animals are doing. See Abolitionism, Neo-welfarism and Incremental reforms.

def: The view that extends moral value to all life, sentient or not.
com: It diverges from sentientism by also including organisms without the capacity to feel, such as plants, in the sphere of direct moral consideration, a relevant point of disagreement between the two currents.

def: A branch of applied ethics that investigates moral questions related to the life sciences and health, including animal research, biotechnology and medicine.
com: Traditionally centered on human dilemmas, bioethics has been pressed by sentientist currents to fully incorporate the interests of nonhuman animals as moral subjects, and not only as means to human ends.

def: The science that studies living beings, their structure, functioning, origin and evolution; the empirical basis for understanding the physiology, behavior and capacities of animals.
com: It is from biological evidence, and not from intuitions or cultural traditions, that criteria such as the presence of sentience are usually assessed.

def: A proposed field of research to study how animals, especially those living outside human control, are positively and negatively affected in their well-being.
com: The expression comes from the economist Yew-Kwang Ng, in the article "Towards Welfare Biology" (1995), and was developed by Catia Faria and Oscar Horta in the chapter "Welfare Biology" of the Routledge Handbook of Animal Ethics (2020). It would be an interdisciplinary field, bringing together ecology, animal welfare science, zoology and veterinary science, to study what is better or worse for each animal as a sentient individual, not as a member of a species, including the natural harms that most wild animals suffer. It is not the same as animal welfare science, which measures physiological and behavioural indicators mainly in animals under human control, such as farmed and laboratory animals, nor as conservation biology, compassionate conservation and conservation welfare, which look at welfare only within conservation goals, a distinction drawn by Luciano Carlos Cunha in Razões para ajudar (2022, in Portuguese). Ng's conclusion that suffering predominates in nature was revised by Zach Groff and Ng himself in 2019, who found an error in the model and concluded that the balance is uncertain, and Heather Browning and Walter Veit (2023) dispute the evidence that wild lives are predominantly bad; it is precisely to answer these doubts that the field proposes empirical research, now funded by organizations such as Wild Animal Initiative. See Wild animal suffering, Animal welfare, Conservation biology, Compassionate conservation and Conservation welfare.

def: A purée made from cooked green banana, used as a thickener and as a substitute for fat and egg in vegan recipes.
The deliberate refusal to consume products or support companies as a form of ethical, economic or political pressure.
A strategy of economic pressure through consumption choices.
A device that wraps an animal's snout to restrict its ability to bite or open its mouth.
An instrument used for bloodless castration of males, by crushing the spermatic cord without an incision.
com: "Bloodless" means without blood, not without pain: the clamp crushes the spermatic cord through the skin, and studies record signs of acute and prolonged pain. Like castration with a rubber ring or a knife, burdizzo castration is allowed without anaesthesia in young animals in many countries; in the United Kingdom, for example, in calves and lambs up to a certain age. See Castration and Anesthesia.

def: A restraint placed on an animal's head (usually a horse) to guide or tie it.
The killing of wild animals, for subsistence, population control or sport.
com: In Brazil, the 1967 Wildlife Protection Law generally prohibits hunting wild animals, with exceptions such as the control of wild boar, an invasive alien species; in countries such as the United States and much of Europe, recreational hunting is legal and regulated. The population-control justification is disputed, because overpopulation often results from human actions, such as the removal of predators, and non-lethal methods such as contraception are in use. Hunting also wounds animals that escape and die later. From a sentientist point of view, subsistence hunting, where there is no alternative, is treated differently from hunting for leisure. See Sport hunting, Subsistence and Animal population control.

def: A form of hunting for leisure or trophies, with no subsistence purpose.
com: It includes trophy hunting, in which the hunter pays to kill large animals, such as lions, elephants and rhinoceroses, and takes body parts as a souvenir. Supporters say the fees fund conservation and local communities; critics, including some conservationists, question how much of that money actually reaches those ends. The killing of Cecil the lion in Zimbabwe in 2015 caused protests worldwide and led airlines to stop carrying trophies. From a sentientist point of view, conserving a species does not justify killing an individual for fun. See Hunting, Safari and Selective outrage.

def: A drink made from roasted and ground corn, used as a substitute for regular coffee.
A narrow individual cage used to confine sows during pregnancy, preventing basic movements such as turning around.
com: A sow's pregnancy lasts almost four months, and she may spend much of it in a crate where she cannot turn around, pregnancy after pregnancy. Sweden and the United Kingdom banned these crates in the 1990s, and the European Union, since 2013, allows them only for the first four weeks after service. In Brazil, the 2020 pig welfare rule of the Ministry of Agriculture limits their use to 35 days after service, but gives existing farms until 2045 to switch to group housing. Group housing is better than the crate, but it does not change the rest of the cycle: insemination, farrowing in farrowing crates and slaughter when productivity falls. See Gestation, Animal confinement and Artificial insemination.

def: A narrow compartment used to confine calves destined for veal production, restricting their movement to keep the meat tender.
com: The calf, separated from the mother soon after birth, is kept in a narrow individual pen, often tethered, and fed a low-iron liquid diet to keep the meat pale. The United Kingdom banned these crates in 1990, and the European Union completed its ban in 2007; in the United States, several states have banned them. Veal continues to exist without crates, because it depends on the dairy industry, which produces male calves of no value for milk production. See Veal, Dairy industry and Premature slaughter.

def: An abnormal behavior in which confined animals (such as pigs or birds) bite or peck one another because of stress, boredom or behavioral frustration.
com: The industry's most common response is not to change the conditions that cause the behaviour but to mutilate the animals: the tip of hens' beaks and piglets' tails are cut off. Research points to lack of space, of straw or other materials for rooting and scratching, and genetic selection for productivity as causes. In the European Union, the law prohibits routine tail docking and requires conditions to be changed first, but the rule is poorly enforced in most countries. See Beak trimming, Tail docking and Environmental enrichment.

def: A term from the transport sector that designates live animals carried as merchandise.
com: The term treats animals as merchandise, in a category close to other perishable cargo. For sea voyages, some countries, such as Australia, set a mortality rate above which the voyage must be investigated, which shows that a certain number of deaths is treated as normal. See Live animal transport, Commodification and Euphemism.

def: A natural red dye extracted from dried females of the cochineal insect, used in foods and cosmetics.
com: It is estimated that about 70,000 cochineal insects are needed to produce one pound (about half a kilo) of dye. On labels it appears as carmine, cochineal, carminic acid or E120, in yogurts, drinks, candy and lipsticks, and many people do not know it comes from insects. In 2012, Starbucks stopped using it in strawberry drinks after customer complaints. See Cruelty-free and Insectivory.

def: The muscle tissue and other organs of animals used as food.
com: Everyday language tends to separate meat from the animal: people speak of fillet, rump or breast, not of the dead steer or hen; in English, pork and beef do the same. In Brazil, many people do not count fish and seafood as meat, although they are also animal tissue. People also speak of "producing" meat, as if it were any other commodity, when every piece comes from an animal who was raised and slaughtered, usually very young. See Absent referent, Euphemism and Slaughter.

def: A food product derived from cellular agriculture, presented as an alternative to traditional animal farming.
com: It is also called lab-grown meat ("labmeat"), cell-cultured meat or cultured meat; the name "clean meat", adopted by the Good Food Institute in 2016, has fallen out of use. Production still uses animal cells, taken by biopsy from living animals or from established cell lines, and early culture media used fetal bovine serum, taken from the blood of fetuses of slaughtered cows; serum-free media now exist, such as the one approved in Singapore in 2023. Sale has been authorized in Singapore in 2020, the United States in 2023, Israel in 2024 and Australia in 2025, and banned in Italy in 2023, Hungary in 2025 and several US states, such as Florida, Alabama and Texas. For veganism, the product is not vegan by origin, but it could greatly reduce the breeding and slaughter of animals if it replaced part of livestock farming, which still depends on cost, scale and acceptance; the guide discusses this debate. See Cellular agriculture and Technological veganism.

def: A dish prepared with shredded green jackfruit, whose fibrous texture resembles shredded meat, popular in vegan cooking.
A textured product based on soy protein, used as a substitute for ground or shredded meat.
Meat from calves slaughtered while still young, usually raised in extreme confinement.
com: Veal is largely a by-product of the dairy industry: male calves do not produce milk and are separated from their mothers soon after birth. The individual crates in which many were raised, with no room to turn around, were banned in the United Kingdom in 1990 and in the European Union in 2007, but are still used in other countries. For this reason, someone who stops eating veal but keeps consuming dairy still sustains the same system. See Veal crate, Dairy industry and Weaning.
